question.text: Aravalli Offshore Fund (Cat II feeder from Mauritius) has appointed a domestic Investment Advisor in India to source deals. Which of the following correctly describes the relationship between the Advisor and the Investment Manager?

answer.text: The Investment Advisor has binding authority to execute trades on behalf of the AIF
The Advisor and the Manager must be the same entity for Cat II feeders

The Investment Advisor provides non-binding advice on investment opportunities; the Investment Manager may choose to execute or leave the same, and the Advisor is paid advisory fees BY THE INVESTMENT MANAGER (not the AIF directly)
Advisor fees are charged directly to the LPs as a fund-level expense pass-through

explanation.text: The Logic: Per the chapter, offshore funds may seek investment advisory services, especially for domestic market access. Domestic investment advisors sign advisory agreements and provide industry-specific insights and potential investee companies. IMPORTANTLY, these are NON-BINDING advice and the investment manager may choose to execute or leave. Investment Advisors are paid advisory fees from the investment MANAGER, not directly from the fund. The Trap: The binding-authority option inverts the non-binding nature. The same-entity option invents a rule. The LP-pass-through option wrongly structures the fee — advisor fees are the manager's responsibility (paid from management fee income). Cross-Exam Context: XIX-C covers advisor vs manager distinction. X-A/X-B (Investment Adviser L1/L2) tests SEBI IA Regulations — different regime for retail/client-facing advisers. Manager's Pro-Tip: Since advisor fees come out of your management fee pool, model them carefully — a 30-40 bps advisory bleed on a 150 bps management fee meaningfully reduces GP economics. Structure advisor fees as success-linked where possible to align incentives.
